one_liner: Tiny tokio HTTP/1.1 server and web framework; matches actix-web on hello-world throughput, ahead ~2% only at 512 connections.
what_it_does: A two-crate Rust workspace. micro-http is a low-level HTTP/1.1 connection driver, `HttpConnection::new(reader, writer).process(&handler)`, that works over any tokio AsyncRead/AsyncWrite pair and uses the `http` crate's Request/Response types. micro-web adds a framework on top: a matchit router with method and header filters, extractors (Method, HeaderMap, path params, Query, Form, Json, String/Bytes), responders including SSE, and decorator middleware (cached Date header; gzip/deflate/zstd/brotli response encoding). It is not a drop-in for actix-web: you register routes with `Router::builder().route("/user/{id}", get(handler))` and serve with `Server::builder().router(r).bind(addr).build()?.start().await`, and it has no TLS, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 or WebSocket support.
how_it_is_fast: There is no novel technique; it is a thin layer over tokio that skips work. httparse parses each request head into a stack `MaybeUninit` header array (at most 64 headers). The head is then split off the read buffer once (`BytesMut::split_to().freeze()`), and the URI and every header value become ref-counted `Bytes` slices of it, built with unsafe `HeaderValue::from_maybe_shared_unchecked` to skip re-validation (the code comment credits this trick to actix). The Date header is formatted by a background task every 800 ms and shared through ArcSwap, accepted sockets get TCP_NODELAY, and each connection is one spawned task on the app's tokio runtime (the benchmark used the default multi-thread runtime). The benchmarked 0.3.0 encodes the whole response into a reused per-connection buffer (8 KB initial) and does one write plus flush per response; the unreleased git head (2026-08-01) sends head and body in one vectored write with no flush.
when_to_use: Internal HTTP/1.1 text/JSON services behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, where hello-world throughput about equal to actix-web is enough (about 166-170k req/s on 4 pinned cores in the 2026-09-24 run).

Embedding an HTTP/1.1 endpoint over a custom transport: micro-http's `HttpConnection` takes any AsyncRead + AsyncWrite pair (for example a Unix socket or an in-memory duplex) and a `Handler` that returns `http::Response<B>` with `B: Body<Data = Bytes>`. Its core dependencies are small (httparse, http, bytes, tokio-util).

Studying or forking a compact HTTP/1.1 implementation (about 7,000 lines across both crates' src, including tests and doc comments) that covers chunked and Content-Length bodies in both directions plus Expect: 100-continue.
Prototypes that want axum-style extractor handlers (`async fn h(method: &Method, Json(u): Json<User>) -> String`) and can live with alpha-stage API churn.
when_not_to_use: You need a real throughput win over actix-web. In the current-method run it is 0.95x / 0.99x / 1.02x at 64 / 256 / 512 connections, its p99 latency is 1.6-1.9x worse at every concurrency, and hyper, ohkami and may_minihttp all beat it in the same run.

Directly internet-facing servers. It has no TLS, no HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, no read, idle or header timeouts (so it is exposed to slowloris), and no handling of `Connection: close`. The Bytes, String, Json and Form extractors also buffer the whole request body with no size limit.

Streaming responses (SSE, large downloads) on the crates.io release. 0.3.0 encodes every response frame into an in-memory buffer and writes it to the socket only when the body ends, so SSE events arrive only when the stream closes and large bodies sit fully in RAM. Only the unreleased git head streams.
Services that need graceful shutdown. `Server::start` stops accepting only on Ctrl-C (SIGINT); it does not handle SIGTERM and does not drain open connections.

Production use that needs maturity or lean builds. The README calls it alpha; it has one maintainer, 29 stars and 0 crates.io reverse dependencies; it has no tower middleware and no WebSocket/Upgrade support. micro-web always pulls in zstd (a C library), brotli, flate2 and the dhat heap profiler, none of them optional.

integration.dependencies: micro-http 0.3.0: tokio, tokio-util, httparse, http, http-body, http-body-util, bytes, futures, mime, thiserror, trait-variant, tracing, tracing-subscriber. micro-web 0.3.0 adds matchit, serde, serde_json, serde_urlencoded, serde_qs, flate2, zstd (C library), brotli, dhat, arc-swap, once_cell, async-trait, dynosaur, hlist2, tower-layer, pin-project-lite and faf-http-date, all non-optional.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.90 (MSRV; edition 2024); CI tests 1.90, stable, beta and nightly
integration.platforms: Anywhere tokio runs, in principle; CI covers ubuntu-latest only, and other platforms are not documented
integration.thread_safety: Handlers must be Send + Sync (micro-http `Handler: Sync` with Send futures); the Server and its router are shared across tasks through an Arc. Each connection is one tokio task, and requests on a connection are handled one at a time.

gotchas: `Server::start()` installs its own global tracing subscriber at WARN level with `set_global_default(...).expect(...)`, so it panics if your app has already installed one. It also `unwrap()`s `set_nodelay` and address resolution. If you need control over these, drive micro-http's `HttpConnection` yourself.

The response header encoder calls `status.canonical_reason().unwrap()`, so a status code with no canonical reason (for example a custom 5xx/4xx) panics the connection task. Responses whose version is not HTTP/1.1 are rejected as Unsupported.

`EncodeDecorator` compresses gzip and deflate at `Compression::best()` (level 9), which is CPU-heavy, and turns the response into a chunked stream. It checks for Content-Encoding on the request rather than the response, so a body the handler has already compressed can be encoded twice.

Version trap. Published 0.3.0, the version the benchmark ran, buffers whole responses (see above). The git head fixes streaming, but since 2026-01-19 it passes the request body as a raw-pointer vtable (`unsafe impl Send for StreamingReqBody`), and `ReqBody` has no lifetime, so moving it out of the handler (for example into `tokio::spawn`) can outlive its backing state. The README Quick Start still pins `micro-web = "0.1"`, and 0.1.1 fails to compile on Rust 1.92 (issue #3).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same 2026-09-24 run, hyper 1.5 (also tokio) beat micro-web at all three concurrencies (173.6k / 168.8k / 166.6k vs 169.6k / 166.6k / 166.4k req/s), and may_minihttp (194k at c=512) and ohkami-nio (182k) were clearly faster. Pick micro-web only if you specifically want its small codebase and extractor-style API over hyper's bare service API; choose may_minihttp or ohkami for throughput and actix-web or hyper for maturity.
verified_claims_summary: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks ran micro-web 0.3.0 from crates.io against actix-web 4.8 on 2026-09-24 (develop f673364). Setup: zrk closed-loop keep-alive, 15 s per level, averaging hello-world GET /, GET /user/0 and POST /user; both built with Rust 1.98, LTO, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort; server pinned to 4 cores of an undisclosed 16-thread x86-64 Linux host whose 'M1' CPU label is hard-coded. Results were 169,642 / 166,580 / 166,409 vs 179,203 / 168,270 / 163,415 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections (0.95x / 0.99x / 1.02x), with micro-web's p99 1.6-1.9x higher (0.65 vs 0.40 ms at c=64, 6.03 vs 3.22 ms at c=512). The 1.11-1.17x lead cited elsewhere comes only from the superseded 2026-09-20 master snapshot.
status_note: Actively committed alpha with one maintainer: last commit 2026-08-01, but the last crates.io release is 0.3.0 from 2025-10-03, so the benchmark did not include the newer write-path change. Dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 per Cargo.toml and the README (GitHub shows only Apache-2.0).
